sections.title: Produce Obligated in Terumot and Ma'asrot
sections.html:
According to most Rishonim, only the five species of grain, wine and oil, which are the important foods for a person, are obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot by Torah law, as it is stated (Devarim 18:4): "The first of your grain, your wine and your oil" (Rashi, Tosafot, Rash, Rashba, Ran and Ritva). From grain the basic food is prepared, such as bread and mezonot (grain-based foods); wine gladdens and nourishes; and olive oil is very nourishing and enriches flavors. In the days of King Ḥizkiya, they added an enactment to separate terumot u-ma'asrot also from other tree fruits and from the various legumes and vegetables.

Some say that legumes and tree fruits are also obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot by Torah law, as it is stated regarding ma'aser sheni (Vayikra 27:30): "And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the tree, is the Lord's…" And it is also stated (Devarim 14:22): "You shall surely tithe all the produce of your seed that the field brings forth year by year" (Yerushalmi Ma'asrot 1:1; Rambam; Rash Sirilio). Although the Torah explicitly mentioned three species, its intention was to teach us the general rule through them. From grain we learn that all kinds of legumes are also obligated, and from grapes and olives we learn that all tree fruits are obligated. And the Sages added an enactment to separate terumot u-ma'asrot also from all kinds of vegetables.

But whatever does not grow from the ground, such as milk and meat, is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot. Although animals feed on grass, meat and milk are not considered produce of the field but rather secondary growths. Likewise, mushrooms are exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot, since they do not grow from the soil. Likewise, plant species that people do not usually eat, but are animal fodder, or are intended to season human food but are not eaten by themselves, are exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot (as explained in the next halakha).1

By Torah law, a person must separate terumot u-ma'asrot from produce that he picks and gathers for his household's food, as it is stated (Devarim 14:22-23): "You shall surely tithe all the produce of your seed… and you shall eat." And by rabbinic law, one is obligated to separate terumot u-ma'asrot also from produce that a person picks in order to sell. Produce whose processing has not been completed, such as grapes to make wine from them or olives to make oil from them – if the buyer makes wine and oil from them for his household's use, they become obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot by Torah law, and if in order to sell them, by rabbinic law (Bava Metzi'a 88b; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 2:1-2).

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Details of the Laws
sections.html:
Any human food that grows from the land is obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot, whether it is eaten in its natural form, or mashed, or made into juice. But parts of the fruit that are not considered human food are exempt. Therefore, peels and seeds that are not fit to be eaten are exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot, and those that are fit to be eaten, such as apple peel and watermelon seeds, are obligated. Grape leaves picked for food, as a wrapping for rice and meat, are exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot, since they are generally not considered food.

Spices that serve only to give flavor, fragrance or color, such as black pepper, cinnamon, cumin, coffee beans and tea leaves, are exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot, since they are not eaten by themselves. But parsley and coriander leaves, which are usually mixed into salad, are obligated, since they are recognizable in their form in the salad and consequently are considered to be eaten by themselves. One who cooks soup with parsley, garlic and onion, even though his intention is that they only give flavor and afterwards he throws them away – the soup is obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot, since its flavor comes from vegetables that are usually eaten in their own form as well.2

Plants intended for medicinal use, fragrance or decoration are exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot. Likewise, khat leaves are exempt. One who grows seeds that are not fit to be eaten in order to grow vegetables, such as onion seeds, they are exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot. One who takes seeds and sprouts them need not tithe the sprouts. Although some are stringent, the main view is that of the lenient.3

Species that are eaten by animals, even if there is a person who wishes to eat them and sowed them for his own consumption, since they are animal fodder, are exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot. But species that are sometimes eaten by people and sometimes by animals, such as barley – if he sowed and gathered them for people, they are obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot, and if he sowed and gathered them for animals, they are exempt (see Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 2:2; Ma'adanei Eretz, Terumot 2:7).4

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Hefker
sections.html:
Hefker (ownerless) produce, that is, produce that any person may take, is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot, for it is stated (Devarim 14:29): "And the Levite, because he has no portion or inheritance with you, shall come" – specifically from produce in which he has no portion or inheritance must one separate terumot u-ma'asrot, but from hefker produce, since he does have a portion and inheritance in it, one does not separate terumot u-ma'asrot (Yerushalmi Terumot 1:3; Ma'asrot 1:1). Therefore, hikers who picked fruit growing wild in a place that belongs to no one may eat it in the field or at home without separating terumot u-ma'asrot from it.

Fruit trees planted for decoration in public gardens that belong to the municipality or to a public association – as long as those responsible for the gardens allow anyone to pick the fruit without restriction, the fruit is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot. And if the matter is not clear, they should inform three people that the fruit is hefker, and thereby the fruit will be exempt without doubt.

One who wishes to declare his produce hefker must say before three people: "My produce is hefker," and thereby it becomes hefker, and anyone may acquire it. At least two of the listeners must be fit to testify, so that if the third comes to acquire the produce, the two can testify that he acquired it lawfully (SA ḤM 273:7). If he declared the produce hefker for the poor and not for the rich, or even declared it hefker for everyone except one person, it is not hefker and one must separate terumot u-ma'asrot from it (Mishna Pe'a 6:1).

The hefker that exempts produce from tithes is from the time it reached "onat ha-ma'asrot" (the tithing stage), that is, it became fit to be eaten in a pressing situation (below, halakha 6), until it was picked and became "fixed for tithes" (below, halakha 7). If he declared his produce hefker while it was still attached to the trees, but not his field, the produce is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:12). But if he declared the field hefker and not the produce, the produce is obligated. Likewise, one who sows a hefker field – even though the field remains hefker, since the produce is his, the produce is obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 2:11).

If he declared his produce hefker, even for one hour, anyone who acquired it is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot, and the owner of the produce cannot retract the hefker after another person has acquired it. But if no other person acquired it, the Sages enacted that as long as three days have not passed since the hefker, the owner of the produce may retract the hefker and annul it, or acquire the produce by lifting it, and the produce will be obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot. Only if the produce remains ownerless for three days, and afterwards he goes back and acquires it, will he be exempt from separating terumot u-ma'asrot from it. The reason for the enactment is to block swindlers who would declare their produce hefker for a short while and immediately reacquire it, and in truth did not intend to make it ownerless but only to exempt themselves from the obligation of terumot u-ma'asrot.5

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Neta Reva'i, Shevi'it and Gifts to the Poor
sections.html:
The fruit of neta reva'i is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot. As is known, the fruit that grows in the first three years of a tree is forbidden under the law of orla, and the fruit of the fourth year is neta reva'i fruit; it is holy, and it is a mitzva to eat it in purity in Jerusalem (above 2:9). Since it is consecrated to its mitzva, one does not leave leket, shikheḥa and pe'a from it for the poor, and one does not separate terumot u-ma'asrot from it (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni Ve-neta Reva'i 9:4). Fruit that is possibly neta reva'i and possibly of the fifth year – one separates terumot u-ma'asrot from it without a blessing, but there is no obligation to give the ma'aser rishon to the Levite and the ma'aser ani to the poor person, since these are monetary obligations, and as with every monetary obligation, without clear proof that one is indeed obligated to pay this debt, there is no obligation to pay it (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 13:20-21).

Produce that grows in the seventh year is hefker and exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot.6

Produce of leket, shikheḥa, pe'a, peret and olelot (gleanings, forgotten sheaves, the corner of the field, fallen grapes and underdeveloped grape clusters) that must be left for the poor is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot.7

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Onat Ha-ma'asrot and the Reckoning of the Years
sections.html:
The mitzva of separating terumot u-ma'asrot applies only after the completion of the work of gathering the produce and its becoming fixed for tithes (below halakhot 6-7). However, "onat ha-ma'asrot" (the tithing stage), according to which the tithing year is determined, is fixed by the time the produce emerges from the unripe stage and reaches the stage at which it can be eaten in a pressing situation. This is the time called "hevi'u shelish" (reaching a third) in grain and legumes, that is, they have reached a third of their ripening and have become fit to be eaten in a pressing situation; and it is the time of ḥanata in tree fruit. A sign of onat ha-ma'asrot is that from that stage, if one sows the grain or the legumes or the seeds in the fruit, they will sprout.8

Onat ha-ma'asrot determines the tithing year for tree fruit, grain and legumes (but not vegetables). Produce that reached onat ha-ma'asrot before its Rosh Ha-shana belongs to the previous year; after its Rosh Ha-shana, to the following year. Two fundamental halakhot depend on this.

The first: one must separate terumot u-ma'asrot from produce of the same year, as it is stated (Devarim 14:22): "You shall surely tithe all the produce of your seed that the field brings forth year by year" – "this teaches that one does not tithe from one year on behalf of another" (Sifrei there). And if he separated from the produce of one year on behalf of another, his actions are void (Mishna Terumot 1:5; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 5:11).

The second: in years 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the Shemita cycle one separates ma'aser sheni, and in years 3 and 6 one separates ma'aser ani, and the time that determines the year with regard to the produce is onat ha-ma'asrot.

The Rosh Ha-shana for grain and legumes is 1 Tishrei. Whatever reached onat ha-ma'asrot before 1 Tishrei belongs to the previous year, and whatever reached onat ha-ma'asrot after 1 Tishrei belongs to the following year.

The Rosh Ha-shana for tree fruit is postponed by four and a half months to Tu Bi-Shvat, because any fruit that reached ḥanata before Tu Bi-Shvat, such as citrus fruit, is known to have grown by virtue of the rains of the past year, and therefore its law is that of the past year. And if it reached ḥanata after Tu Bi-Shvat, like most fruit, its law is that of the new year, since it grew by virtue of this year's rains. However, in the seventh year, the year for trees begins on 1 Tishrei, so that whatever reached ḥanata from 1 Tishrei until Tu Bi-Shvat of the seventh year is hefker and exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot, and whatever reached ḥanata from 1 Tishrei until Tu Bi-Shvat in the year after the seventh has the law of the first year (Pe'at Ha-shulḥan 22, n. 14; Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it 3, n. 6).

For vegetables the law is different. The Rosh Ha-shana for vegetables is 1 Tishrei, as for grain and legumes, but their onat ha-ma'asrot is at the time of their harvesting, and not "from when they reached a third." This is because they grow through irrigation, and consequently can be grown in all seasons of the year; therefore it is not their growth that determines, but their harvesting. In addition, they do not ripen all at once, so that if the year were determined by the stage at which the produce is fit to be eaten in a pressing situation, it is possible that within one field some of the vegetables would belong to the previous year and some to the following year, without its being possible to distinguish between them. Therefore the Sages established that their tithing year is determined by the time of their harvesting, which is a clear time. And the same law applies to rice, millet and sesame (Rosh Ha-shana 14a).

The etrog, too, like vegetables, grows on all waters, for when it is irrigated it continues to grow beyond its natural season, and therefore its tithing year is determined by the time it is picked. However, since it is a tree, its Rosh Ha-shana is on Tu Bi-Shvat. But the law of other citrus fruits is like that of other trees, whose year is determined by ḥanata, since they have a fixed season in which they grow and are picked.9

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Gemar Melakha
sections.html:
Even though the produce was picked after it reached onat ha-ma'asrot, as long as its processing has not been completed ("nigmera melakhtam"), one should not separate terumot u-ma'asrot from it, because it has not yet reached its choicest stage. In addition, only after "gemar melakha" (completion of processing) is it possible to calculate properly what must be separated for the tithes.10

Gemar melakha is the completion of the work of gathering the produce from the field and preparing it for bringing home or for sale. For produce that is usually cleaned in the field, gemar melakha is after it is cleaned and its gathering is completed. When one intends to make wine from the grapes and oil from the olives, gemar melakha is upon completing the preparation of the wine and the oil; when one intends to eat the grapes fresh, gemar melakha is upon completing their gathering, and if as raisins – when they become raisins; and when one intends to eat the olives pickled, gemar melakha is at the end of their pickling. Gemar melakha for wheat is the "miru'aḥ" (smoothing of the pile), that is, after the stalks have been threshed to separate the grain kernels from them, and they have been winnowed in the wind to remove the chaff, and the remaining waste has been sorted out, and the wheat kernels have been properly set down in their place.

Although it is forbidden to separate terumot u-ma'asrot from produce that has not reached gemar melakha, after the fact, if one separated, he has fulfilled his obligation. Sometimes there is doubt as to when gemar melakha is, for example with produce that is usually gathered in the field into crates and afterwards undergoes cleaning, sorting and packing in the packing house in preparation for marketing. Ab initio one should resolve the doubt and wait until the packing is completed; but if there is a need to separate terumot u-ma'asrot earlier – because afterwards they may forget to separate from it, or afterwards it will be packed in a way that makes it difficult to separate from it, or perhaps the workers will take some of it home without separating terumot u-ma'asrot – it is proper to separate terumot u-ma'asrot from it after completing the first stage of gathering.11

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: The Law of Produce in the Stages of Becoming Fixed for Tithes
sections.html:
By Torah law, only after the processing of the produce is completed and it becomes fixed for tithes by being brought into the house is one obligated to separate terumot u-ma'asrot from it. As it is stated (Devarim 26:13): "I have removed the holy things from the house" – thus the Torah mitzva applies only to produce that has reached the house (Bava Metzi'a 88a). That is, although it is permitted ab initio to separate terumot u-ma'asrot from produce whose processing has been completed, the Torah prohibition of eating from it without separating terumot u-ma'asrot begins only from the time it is brought into the house.

The Sages added a safeguard to the Torah and established two halakhot:

The first: already from the time the produce has been picked, even though it has not yet become fixed for tithes, it is forbidden to eat from it in a fixed manner (akhilat keva), and it is forbidden to sow it in the ground. Only eating from it casually (arai), or feeding it to animals in a fixed manner, is permitted before the produce has become fixed for tithes (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 3:1-2; 20; 6:3).

The second: that the produce becomes fixed for tithes even before it is brought into the house. For if the owner of the field intends to sell it, immediately after its gemar melakha it becomes fixed for tithes, and it will be forbidden to eat from it even casually as long as terumot u-ma'asrot have not been separated from it. And even though in practice the produce has not yet reached the places where it will be sold, since its processing has already been completed, and if a buyer comes they will sell to him, it has become fixed for tithes. But if even when a buyer comes they will not sell to him, it is permitted to eat from it casually until it reaches the place where they intend to sell it, and it becomes fixed for tithes (Mishna Ma'asrot 2:3, Rash, Ra'av, Rash Sirilio; Yerushalmi Ma'asrot 1:4).

And if the owner of the produce intends to bring it to his house for eating, the Sages enacted that even before he brings it into his house, it becomes fixed for tithes through one of six additional things, and it will be forbidden to eat from it even casually without first separating terumot u-ma'asrot from it. These are the six things: 1) bringing it into a guarded courtyard; 2) mekaḥ – selling it; 3) cooking;
4) salting or pickling; 5) separating teruma gedola from it; 6) Shabbat – with the onset of Shabbat, produce designated for eating on Shabbat becomes fixed for tithes (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 3:3; 4:1-2).

One who is in doubt whether his eating is fixed or casual, or whether the produce has become fixed for tithes, should separate terumot u-ma'asrot from it with a blessing and thereby resolve the doubt.12

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Produce Growing in a Courtyard
sections.html:
Produce that grows in a guarded courtyard, which no stranger may enter, may be eaten casually only before its gemar melakha, that is, before it is gathered – for example, one grape or one fig, which are eaten in one go. But if he picks two grapes or two figs, or a large fruit that is not eaten in one go, such as an apple or a large fig, already in picking them they are gathered and their processing is completed, and they become obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot, for this is the manner of gathering them in a courtyard. And since they are inside a guarded courtyard, which fixes them for tithes, they are forbidden even in casual eating before he separates terumot u-ma'asrot from them (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 4:15; 17; Radbaz there 18).

If he climbed a tree and picked many fruits there in a way that completed their processing, as long as he is on the tree and has not come down to the ground of the guarded courtyard, the produce has not yet become fixed for tithes, and since his eating on the tree is casual eating, he may eat from it without separating terumot u-ma'asrot (Rambam there).

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: The Place of the Obligation in the Land of Israel
sections.html:
The mitzva of terumot u-ma'asrot is one of the mitzvot dependent on the Land, for everything that grows within the territory of the Land of Israel, including the eastern side of the Jordan and Syria, is included in the mitzva. However, when the majority of the Jewish people dwell in the Land, the obligation of the mitzva is from the Torah, and when the majority of the people are not in the Land, as in our situation today, the obligation of the mitzva is rabbinic. And some hold that in places settled by those who came up from Babylonia in the days of the Second Temple, even when the majority of the people is not in the Land, the obligation is from the Torah (below 12:11-12; Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it Ve-yovel 11:4 explains who is included in the count of the Jewish people for the law of the majority).

All the territories under the rule of the State of Israel are obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot with a blessing, and one may separate terumot u-ma'asrot from produce growing in one place on behalf of produce growing in another place. However, it is proper not to separate from produce growing in territories of the Land of Israel under foreign rule, such as Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Egypt, on behalf of produce growing in the State of Israel, and vice versa, because some hold that in the territories under Israeli rule the basis of the mitzva is from the Torah, and in the territories outside the borders of the State the basis of the mitzva is rabbinic. When the majority of Israel dwells in the Land, the obligation of the mitzva will be from the Torah in all the territories under Israeli rule (this topic is explained at length below 12:17).

Produce of the Land of Israel that is exported abroad – if its processing was completed in the Land, it is obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot, and if its processing was completed abroad, it is exempt. And if at the time of picking he intended to export it abroad, even if its processing was completed in the Land, some say it is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot (Maharsham), and some are stringent (Ḥazon Ish, Igrot Moshe). Since the law is rabbinic, those who wish to be lenient may do so.13

Produce from abroad that entered the Land – if its processing was completed abroad, it is exempt, and if its processing was completed in the Land, it is obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot by rabbinic law (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 1:22). Several Aḥaronim wrote that all this is on condition that the produce grew in a Jew's field, but produce that grew abroad in a gentile's field, even if its processing was completed in the Land, is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot (Aḥi'ezer, Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach). And although some are stringent (Ḥazon Ish), since the law is rabbinic, and so it seems, the halakha follows the lenient view.14

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Produce of a Gentile
sections.html:
A gentile who has land in the Land of Israel, and grew produce on it, and picked and gathered it – the produce is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot (Bekhorot 11b; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 1:11). And if he sold the produce to a Jew before its gemar melakha, and the Jew completed the work of gathering it, the produce is obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot. For the halakha is that a gentile's ownership does not remove his land from the mitzvot; therefore, even though the produce grew in a gentile's land, since it was in a Jew's possession at its gemar melakha, which is the stage at which it becomes obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot, it is obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot. However, regarding the giving of ma'aser rishon and ma'aser ani, one gives only according to the percentage of the produce that grew in the Jew's possession, as explained in the note.15

Produce of a Jew's field that gentile workers picked and whose gathering they completed is obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot by rabbinic law. Produce of a gentile's field that Jewish workers picked and whose gathering they completed – according to most poskim, one is obligated to separate terumot u-ma'asrot; but since some are lenient, one should separate terumot u-ma'asrot without a blessing.16

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: More Laws Concerning a Gentile
sections.html:
A Jew who sold his produce to a gentile before gemar melakha – even though by Torah law the produce is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot, the Sages enacted that it be obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot. This is because of "ba'alei kisim," that is, wealthy people, who, in order to evade giving terumot u-ma'asrot, would sell their produce to a gentile before gemar melakha. To prevent them from doing so, the Sages enacted that even if the gentile completes the work of gathering it, the produce will be obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot. Only if the Jew sells his produce to a gentile while it is still on the trees, before it reaches onat ha-ma'asrot, that is, before it is fit to be eaten in a pressing situation, and it remains in the gentile's possession until after gemar melakha, will the produce be exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot (Menaḥot 67a, Rashi and Rash; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 1:13, Radbaz).

When a Jew and a gentile are partners in a field, the produce is obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot. To resolve the doubt, it is good for them to divide the field in advance, so that the gentile's part will be exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot and the Jew's part will be obligated. After the fact, if they did not do so, they should divide the produce between them, and the Jew should separate from his share (SA 331:11, and see the Harḥavot).

A gentile is exempt from separating terumot u-ma'asrot from produce that grew in his field in the Land of Israel, and he also cannot separate terumot u-ma'asrot on behalf of a Jew. But if he wishes, he may volunteer to separate terumot u-ma'asrot from his produce (Mishna Terumot 3:9, Yerushalmi 3:5). Some say this is a rabbinic enactment (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 4:15; SA 331:44). And some say that this is the law by Torah law, for just as a gentile can consecrate a sacrifice, so he can separate terumot u-ma'asrot from produce he grew in the Land of Israel (Rashi, Tosafot; see Har Tzvi OḤ 2:2).

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Places That Are Not a Field
sections.html:
By Torah law, only what grows in the ground is obligated in terumot u-ma'asrot, and what grows in a perforated pot is also considered to grow in the ground. But what grows in a pot without a hole, or on substrates that separate it from the ground, is exempt. And the Sages obligated it in terumot u-ma'asrot with a blessing (Yoma 83b).

What grows inside a house, even though its floor is earth, is exempt from terumot u-ma'asrot (Ra'avad). According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:10), although by Torah law it is indeed exempt, by rabbinic law it is obligated; therefore one should separate terumot u-ma'asrot without a blessing.

One is obligated to separate terumot u-ma'asrot from produce that grows in greenhouses.17

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Demai and Other Doubts
sections.html:
In the language of the Sages, "tevel" is produce from which terumot u-ma'asrot have not been separated, and the meaning of "tevel" is "tov-lo" ("not good"), that is, this produce is not yet good for eating. "Demai" is produce about which there is doubt whether terumot u-ma'asrot were separated from it. "Demai" is an Aramaic word whose translation is "What is this?" That is, there is a question about this produce: is it tithed?

In the time of the Sages, most amei ha-aretz would separate terumot u-ma'asrot, but since some of them did not separate them properly, the Sages enacted that the produce of amei ha-aretz would have the status of demai: teruma gedola is not separated from it, because its separation was widespread among the amei ha-aretz, but ma'aser rishon, terumat ma'aser, and ma'aser sheni or ani are separated. However, in practice, even though they separated the ma'aser rishon and ma'aser ani produce by designating a place, the Sages did not obligate giving them to the Levite and the poor person. For they are monetary obligations, to which the rule applies: "The burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow"; and unless the Levite or the poor person proves that tithes were indeed not separated from this produce, they need not be given. But from the ma'aser rishon one must separate terumat ma'aser and give it to the kohen, since it has sanctity and an Israelite is forbidden to eat it. Likewise regarding ma'aser sheni, since it has sanctity, one must separate it and eat it in Jerusalem in purity. One does not recite a blessing on the separation of terumot u-ma'asrot and the redemption of ma'aser sheni from demai produce, according to the well-known rule: "In a doubt about blessings, one is lenient" (see Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 9:1-4). And if one redeems ma'aser sheni of demai, there is no need to add a fifth (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni 5:4).

Today, when a doubt arises about produce whether it is tithed, the doubt also concerns teruma gedola, since amei ha-aretz do not separate it either. Therefore one should separate all the terumot u-ma'asrot without a blessing; however, as stated, the monetary obligations – ma'aser rishon and ma'aser ani – need not be given to the Levite and the poor person, whereas the sanctified terumot must, because of the doubt, be placed wrapped in the trash bin, and the ma'aser sheni must be redeemed on a peruta.

Whenever a person is in doubt whether the produce before him belongs to a ma'aser sheni year or a ma'aser ani year, he should separate both tithes because of the doubt and say: "If it is obligated in ani, let it be ma'aser ani, and if in sheni, let it be sheni." He should redeem the ma'aser sheni on a peruta and give the ma'aser ani to a poor person. And one who wishes to be lenient may separate ma'aser sheni alone.18
